Neuf ans après l’attentat de Québec : pr: Nine Years After the Quebec City Attack: Praying Between Vigilance and Resilience
Neuf ans après l’attentat de Québec, les: Nine years after the Quebec City attack, Muslims speak about fear, vigilance and the gaps in mosque security.
Un fidèle en prière à la Grande Mosquée: A worshipper prays at the Grande Mosquée de Québec (Centre culturel islamique de Québec) during the January 29, 2026 commemoration, nine years after the terrorist attack that claimed the lives of six worshippers.
La préparation de cet article s’est insc: This article was prepared in a delicate context, marked both by the weight of memory and by a climate of mistrust that is still very much present within some of Quebec's Muslim communities. On several occasions, my reporting efforts ran up against reluctance, notably from mosque committees that were unwilling to speak publicly about current issues related to security and the social climate.
Cette réserve s’explique en partie par u: This reserve is explained in part by a conviction shared by some of the people we met: that it is sometimes better to keep a low profile, avoid any media exposure and “not make waves,” for fear of drawing negative attention or reviving tensions. This context limited access to certain sources and explains the absence of some voices in this article, particularly those from Montréal neighbourhoods where Muslim communities live.
Par ailleurs, afin de documenter le plus: Moreover, in order to document lived realities as faithfully as possible, the fieldwork required a trip to Quebec City. I attended the three days of commemoration organized by the Centre culturel islamique de Québec, the mosque targeted in the January 29, 2017 attack. I also visited the site of the attack and met members of this community, which is still deeply marked by the events.
Les témoignages recueillis s’inscrivent: The testimonies gathered respect the pace, the silences and the limits expressed by the people I met. This article does not claim to be exhaustive, but aims to convey, with rigour and humanity, a climate, perceptions and the concerns of those who agreed to speak.
<strong>Neuf ans après l’attentat terror: Nine years after the terrorist attack on the Grande Mosquée de Québec, the question of security in and around mosques remains a burning one. Between reinforced technical measures, police cooperation deemed generally adequate and a persistent sense of insecurity among some worshippers, the testimonies gathered paint a portrait of a community torn between vigilance, worry and resilience, in a context marked by a rise in hate crimes and a political climate perceived as anxiety-inducing. A report.
À la veille de la commémoration du neuvi: On the eve of the commemoration of the ninth anniversary of the terrorist attack on the Grande Mosquée de Québec, <l1>a call to demonstrate in front of a Montréal mosque</l1> on the very day of the memorial ceremonies revived concerns. For many Muslims in Quebec, such a call is part of a broader climate of rising Islamophobia, fuelled by political and media discourse perceived as stigmatizing, and it weighs heavily on the sense of safety around places of worship.
L’appel à manifester, présenté comme une: The call to demonstrate, presented as a mobilization “for secularism in our schools and our streets,” circulated on social media under the name “Alexandre Bissonnette,” which is none other than the name of the perpetrator of the attack on the Grande Mosquée. The choice of this pseudonym, as well as of the location and timing of the demonstration, deeply shocked the Muslim community.
Pour Nabila D., qui fréquente plusieurs: For Nabila D., who attends several mosques in Quebec City, this episode illustrates the prevailing climate, which she describes as “toxic.” “You see a climate of hatred, of intimidation, threatening looks, and even more so when it's a visible place of worship,” she says. In her view, social media play a central role in spreading hateful speech. It often happens under the cover of anonymity, but its effects are felt in everyday life.
<l1>L’attentat de 2017 a placé le Canada: <l1>The 2017 attack put Canada at the top of the G7 countries with the most targeted killings of Muslims</l1>. Nine years after the Quebec City attack, the fear that a similar scenario could happen again remains present among some worshippers. “Yes, in my opinion, it can happen again in one way or another,” says Nabila, who points to rising tensions and a normalization of hostile discourse toward Muslims.
Cette peur est partagée par Salam El-Mou: This fear is shared by Salam El-Mousawi, a worshipper at the Ahl-ul-bayt mosque in Côte-des-Neiges. He points out that mosques are, by nature, open places, which makes them vulnerable. “The Ahl-ul-bayt mosque, like other mosques, welcomes peaceful worshippers who sometimes feel a certain unease,” he says. “They keep an eye on the people present, because mosques are generally open to everyone, which makes infiltration easy and allows anyone to commit, God forbid, any kind of act. That is why everyone makes an effort to be vigilant and to watch over the worshippers so that what happened in Quebec City doesn't happen again.”
<strong>Entre sentiment d’insécurité et: Between a feeling of insecurity and quiet resistance
« Il y a un avant et un après l’installa: “There is a before and an after the installation of the security system,” sums up Boufeldja Bouabdallah, co-founder of the Centre culturel islamique de Québec, speaking of the lasting impact of the 2017 attack on attendance at the Grande Mosquée and on worshippers' relationship to their places of prayer. According to him, in the months following the tragedy, many families stopped coming, notably those who took part in educational activities for children. Then, after the arson attack on the car of the centre's president the following year, “we, as individuals, didn't look for absolute security, but the mosque, we wanted to secure it,” he says.
L’établissement a ainsi entrepris l’inst: The centre therefore began installing electronic systems: doors locked with access-card chips, sensors, and cameras inside and outside the building. Thanks to this security system, combined with an occasional police presence around the building, “people felt reassured. Little by little, they started coming back to the mosque,” he observes, describing a slow but noticeable resumption of community life.
Rencontrée lors de la cérémonie de commé: Met at the ninth-anniversary commemoration ceremony organized by the City of Québec at the former Sainte-Foy city hall, Amel Henchiri, president of the Association de la mosquée de Beauport, recounts the shock of the evening of January 29, 2017. “I told myself that if I didn't go to the mosque the next day, I would live with post-traumatic stress for the rest of my life,” she confides. For her, going back to pray was a way of breaking the terror.
Dans plusieurs mosquées du Québec, des s: In many mosques across Quebec, security systems have been installed over the years – cameras, keypads, access controls – with the help of funding from the Government of Canada through the <l1>Canada Community Security Program (CCSP)</l1>, which was launched in October 2024 and replaced the Security Infrastructure Program (SIP).
Salam El-Mousawi confirme que sa mosquée: Salam El-Mousawi confirms that his mosque received federal funding to improve its security. “Yes, there are cameras and electronic devices, as well as a security system at the entrance and exit (keypad).” But Mr. El-Mousawi qualifies the effect of these initiatives, believing that no technical measure can, on its own, dispel fear. “As you know, these are only minor obstacles. God forbid, they could be bypassed by someone with bad intentions.”
Même constat de la part de Nabila, qui n: Nabila makes the same observation, noting that while many mosques strengthened their security after 2017, some remain less equipped, either because they lack the means or because they are newer.
Ola Shaheen, responsable du marketing au: Ola Shaheen, marketing manager at the Canadian Youth Development Center, says she has spoken with several mosque leaders in Quebec, who told her they shared this sense of insecurity.
« Les subventions existent, mais elles n: “The grants exist, but they aren't always accessible. Many mosques don't know how to apply, or don't have the resources to put together an application.” In her view, improving security also requires better support. “There should be people in the communities to help leaders understand the process, fill out the forms, go after this funding. Otherwise, we're left with incomplete systems.”
Du côté de la représentante spéciale du: The office of Canada's Special Representative on Combatting Islamophobia says the federal program is currently under review in order to better meet the needs of communities. Ottawa says it wants to consult the organizations concerned to improve the accessibility and fairness of the funding.
En décembre dernier, à l’occasion d’une: Last December, during a religious celebration and a family engagement at the Jaffari Community Centre in Thornhill, in suburban Toronto, the atmosphere was festive.
Devant la mosquée, les femmes arrivaient: In front of the mosque, women arrived elegantly dressed, some holding roses. Cars moved slowly past to drop off guests, in an atmosphere both joyful and solemn. Warm greetings, smiles and knowing glances gave the event the feel of an intimate, community celebration.
À l’entrée, la sécurité s’organisait ave: At the entrance, security was organized discreetly. A female officer stood on the women's side, a male officer on the men's side. Both wore bright yellow vests and welcomed worshippers calmly and warmly, guiding guests, answering questions and making sure the evening went smoothly.
Cette présence, à la fois rassurante et: This presence, both reassuring and integrated into community life, did not seem to disturb the festivities. It nonetheless pointed to a deeper reality: even in moments of joy, vigilance remains necessary. The celebration took place under protection and was designed to reassure, without breaking the harmony of the moment.
Des membres de différentes communautés m: Members of different Muslim communities in Quebec were asked whether similar arrangements exist in their mosques. Several replied that this kind of visible human presence, with staff handling reception and security, was rare, even non-existent, in the places of worship they attend. Some instead mentioned measures limited to cameras or locked doors.
Ce contraste fait écho au témoignage d’O: This contrast echoes the testimony of Ola Shaheen, who attends a mosque in western Montréal. She explains that since the 2017 attack, she has been constantly on guard when she goes there.
« Depuis l’attentat de Québec, chaque fo: “Ever since the Quebec City attack, every time I enter a mosque, I feel a sense of insecurity, as if I were waiting for something to happen. It's as if we expect something truly tragic to occur. So when I walk in, I look around… And when I go into the mosque, I always check who is standing near the door,” she confides.
Pour cette femme d’origine palestinienne: For this woman of Palestinian origin, who arrived in Quebec in 2009, there was clearly a before and an after.
« Avant, je me sentais fière d’être musu: “Before, I felt proud to be Muslim here in Canada, so far from my country. Being able to walk into a mosque and find people from my community there was important to me. It was natural, reassuring,” she explains.
Depuis l’attentat, poursuit-elle, ce rap: Since the attack, she continues, that relationship has changed profoundly. “Every time you walk into a mosque, you feel a different kind of fear – this sense that something serious could happen. It's never neutral, it's never unconscious. The attack turned everything upside down.”
Interrogée sur la scène observée à Toron: Asked about the scene observed in Toronto, which we described to her during the interview, Ola Shaheen says she is surprised by the visible presence of security officers. “I've visited at least seven mosques in Quebec, and I've almost never seen guards there. When you tell me what you saw in Toronto, it strikes me. Yet during the times when mosques are very busy, it would be reassuring to have officers on site.”
Elle nuance toutefois : « Il arrive parf: She adds a caveat, however: “Sometimes you see police patrols going by mosques, but they're not really there at the entrances.”
Pour Stephen Brown, président du Conseil: For Stephen Brown, CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims (NCCM), these concerns cannot be separated from the political context in Quebec. “It's hard to say in absolute terms, but Muslim Quebecers clearly experience much more anxiety about their belonging in society,” he says, comparing the situation in Quebec to the one in Ontario.
Selon lui, les débats et les lois provin: In his view, provincial debates and laws, notably around secularism, send a message of exclusion. “The feeling many people have is that, in order to be accepted, they have to make themselves invisible,” he says. According to the NCCM, this perception contributes to a deterioration of social harmony.
Sameer Majzoub, président du Forum musul: Sameer Majzoub, president of the Canadian Muslim Forum, distinguishes between physical security measures and what he calls “deterrence.” Cameras and keypads, he says, are mainly useful after an incident, to document and investigate. “Deterrence is preventing hate upstream,” he explains, calling for public policies and discourse that reduce tensions rather than feed them.
Stephen Brown fait un constat similaire: Stephen Brown makes a similar observation: every time political statements targeting Muslims emerge in the news, the NCCM sees an increase in reports of threats, insults and verbal attacks. Without drawing an automatic link, he underscores the concrete impact of the social climate on people's sense of safety.
Malgré la multiplication des incidents,: Despite the growing number of incidents, official complaints remain few. Among the mosque representatives La Converse contacted for this report, many requested anonymity or simply declined our interview request. Sameer Majzoub points to fear of reprisals, weariness in the face of long and costly procedures, and a sense of futility. “People are afraid, and they're tired,” he sums up.
Cette sous-déclaration des incidents con: This underreporting of incidents contributes, he says, to making the realities lived by Muslims less visible, even as provocative calls, like the one circulated under the name of the perpetrator of the attack on the Grande Mosquée de Québec, continue to circulate.
Neuf ans après l’attentat de Québec, la: Nine years after the Quebec City attack, the January 29 commemoration is no longer limited to remembering the victims. It takes place in a climate where fear, vigilance and a sense of identity-based precariousness remain very present for the Muslim community.
Pour plusieurs personnes interrogées, la: For several of the people interviewed, the security of mosques cannot be separated from a broader issue: social cohesion. “Disagreement is natural, but it must never degenerate into violence,” Salam El-Mousawi reminds us. A reminder all the more necessary because the memory of January 29 remains inseparable from current debates on the place of Muslims in Quebec's public space.
Pour plusieurs fidèles et responsables c: For many worshippers and community leaders, the commemoration thus takes on a dual significance: honouring the memory of those who were lost, while recalling the need for a collective commitment against the normalization of hate. A vigilance that, beyond places of worship, calls on society as a whole.

And with nobody watching, it’s not really reassuring,” she explains.
